103063706.html: When it comes to finding grants to buy a home, the process can feel overwhelming. This lesson will guide you on where to start and how to avoid common mistakes.

103063706.text: Make an Appointment With a HUD Counselor

103063706.html: First, find a HUD-approved housing counselor and make an appointment. Funded by the government, these experts help you navigate the details relevant to your state, region, and situation. Here's how to start:

items.label: Search
items.html: Visit HUD.gov/counseling and search for counselors by entering your zip code.

items.label: Locate
items.html: Pinpoint the application or contact information on the website of the HUD-approved financial counselor you have chosen, and follow the steps indicated to start the process of acquiring a counselor.

items.label: Check Email
items.html: Check your email, where the HUD-approved agency will contact you to schedule an appointment in person, over the phone, or through a Zoom meeting.

items.label: Gather Information
items.html: Gather all the information you need to buy a house.

103063706.html: Create folders to keep all your information ordered and in one place.

103063706.text: Seek Advice from More than One Expert

103063706.html: If one HUD counselor says you're ineligible or is unhelpful, seek another HUD-approved counselor or other comparable resources, such as NeighborWorks. Many programs exist, and no one knows them all.

Another valuable resource is findhelp.org. Look up "home buyer education" to find local nonprofits that can guide you through grant and funding options. These organizations often offer additional support, typically at no cost to you.
Consulting multiple experts boosts your chances of finding the proper support.

103063707.html: It's time to act after your HUD counselor appointment, now that you understand your finances and housing goals.
This lesson focuses on contacting organizations for housing grants and financial assistance. These programs help secure funds for down payments, closing costs, and reduced-price homes.

These programs are part of the "giving economy" — a network of government offices and nonprofits distributing funds at no cost. Unlike for-profit sites on Google, these organizations aim to help, not profit from your search.

items.label: NeighborWorks
items.html: Visit neighborworks.org to find a local branch. NeighborWorks aids homebuyers with local grants, education, and resources.

items.label: State HFA
items.html: State Housing Finance Agency (NCSHA): Visit ncsha.org to locate your state housing finance agency, which provides grants and programs. Call for assistance with your homeownership goals.

items.label: FHLBanks
items.html: Federal Home Loan Banks: Visit fhlbanks.com to find your Federal Home Loan Bank, which offers grants and funding for housing, including down payment assistance. Contact them to explore options.

items.label: Habitat
items.html: Habitat for Humanity: Check habitat.org for local Habitat for Humanity offices. This program helps you purchase a home at a reduced price in exchange for volunteer work, known as "sweat equity."

items.label: USDA RD
items.html: USDA Rural Development (RD): Visit rd.usda.gov for single-family housing programs in rural areas. Contact your local USDA office for information on grants and loans.

items.label: Community Development
items.html: Community Development Offices: Contact your county's Community Development Office for grants to buy or renovate homes using federal funds. Call 211 or visit 211.org for your local office.

items.label: CDFIs
items.html: Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs): Use the CDFI locator at cdfifund.gov to find local banks offering grants for low-income homebuyers.

items.label: FindHelp
items.html: FindHelp.org: Visit findhelp.org to search for local housing programs. The platform connects you with nonprofits offering free resources and grants.

items.label: $1 Houses
items.html: Houses for $1 Program: Look for government initiatives offering foreclosed homes for $1, along with renovation grants. Contact your local HUD office for details: https://www.hudhomestore.gov/

items.label: Housing Authority
items.html: Local Housing Authorities: Contact your local housing authority; they often manage grant programs or partner with nonprofits for housing assistance. Here is the hud.gov link.

103063707.html: Call first: Most of these organizations require direct communication. Call their offices and explain your situation.
Be persistent: Not all programs will be available in your area, so you may need to make several calls to find the right fit.
Stay focused: Avoid Google searches for these resources. Stick to nonprofit and government-backed programs to avoid being redirected to for-profit services.

items.label: Community Development Offices (also check your local government website)
Houses for $1 Program (contact your local HUD office)
Local Housing Authorities (search for your regional housing authority website)

103063707.html: This step sets you on the path to securing the funds you need for your home-buying journey. Start calling today!

79122514.html: Starting a business can feel overwhelming, especially when finding funding, legal guidance, and the proper support. The key? Don’t start by asking for money — begin by asking for help. This lesson will guide you through the best free resources to get expert advice on launching your business correctly.

79122514.text: Make an Appointment With a Free Business Mentor

79122514.html: The first step to success is talking to the right experts. Nonprofit organizations across the country offer free business mentoring, legal assistance, and funding guidance. Here’s how to get started:

items.label: Search
items.html: Visit AmericasSBDC.org, Score.org, and/or SBA.gov/Local-Assistance (under construction) and enter your ZIP code to find nonprofit business advisors near you.

items.label: Locate
items.html: Choose a business mentorship location and check their website for contact details and appointment options.

items.label: Check Email
items.html: After reaching out, you’ll receive an email from your chosen mentor with details for your in-person, phone, or Zoom consultation.

items.label: Gather Information
items.html: Organize your business idea, potential funding needs, and any key questions you have before your appointment.

79122514.html: Create folders to store all your business-related documents in one place.

Not all mentors will have the same insights or solutions. If one doesn’t provide the information you need, don’t stop — seek out another. There are different specialized resources for various business types and backgrounds:

items.html: Veterans | If you’re a veteran, check out the Veterans Business Outreach Center (VBOC) for additional business counseling and resources. Veterans Business Outreach Center (VBOC)
Individuals with Disabilities | Special nonprofit organizations offer tailored business support. National Disability Institute
Rural Businesses & Farmers | Visit Farmers.gov to find grants and programs for small businesses in rural areas.

79122514.html: Beyond expert advisors, networking with other business owners is one of the best ways to gain real-world insights. Find free entrepreneur meetups to learn from those who have already started a business:

items.html: Meetup.com | Enter your ZIP code to find local business groups and networking events.
Entrepreneur Groups | Look for free local meetups like startup workshops, small business owner networking, and industry-specific groups.

79122514.html: Before applying for funding, you must understand the best options for your business idea. Free mentors and entrepreneur groups provide expert advice to save you time, money, and effort.

items.label: Find Free Business Groups on Meetup

79122515.html: It’s time for the next steps after your free business mentor appointment, and you understand your business goals and potential funding sources.

This lesson focuses on contacting organizations that offer grants and financial assistance to help you start or grow your business. These programs provide funding, training, and resources for entrepreneurs.

These programs are part of the “giving economy” — a network of government offices and nonprofits distributing funds for free. Unlike for-profit websites you might find on Google, these organizations exist to help you, not to charge you for services.

items.label: Economic Development
items.html: Economic Development Offices — Visit eda.gov/resources to find your state’s economic development office. These offices distribute grants, loans, and training programs to help businesses grow. Call for funding opportunities in your state.

items.label: APEX
items.html: APEX Accelerators — Visit apexaccelerators.us to connect with APEX Accelerators, a government-funded program that helps businesses secure government contracts — a long-term funding source for your business.

items.label: SSBCI
items.html: SSBCI (State Small Business Credit Initiative) — Visit home.treasury.gov to locate your state’s SSBCI program, which provides grants, loans, and direct investments in small businesses.

items.label: CareerOneStop
items.html: CareerOneStop (Department of Labor) — Visit careeronestop.org to access training grants and funding for entrepreneurs. This program can help train employees or provide funding for you to learn new skills. Also visit the CareerOneStop Business Center.

items.label: CDFIs
items.html: CDFIs (Community Development Financial Institutions) — Use the CDFI locator at cdfifund.gov to find government-backed banks that provide grants and low-interest loans to small businesses.

items.label: Opportunity Network
items.html: Opportunity Network (matched savings grants) — Some organizations match your savings: if you save $1, they add $5 or more to fund your business. Visit cdfifund.gov to find programs in your area.

items.label: Veterans
items.html: Veteran-Owned Business Assistance — If you’re a veteran, there are special grants and funding programs to support your business. Visit sba.gov to find Veteran Business Outreach Centers near you.

items.label: Minority and Women
items.html: Minority & Women-Owned Business Support — There are dedicated grants for women and minority entrepreneurs available through state and nonprofit programs. Visit grants.gov to check eligibility.

items.label: Meetup
items.html: Meetup.com for Entrepreneurs — Networking is essential. Use meetup.com to find local entrepreneur groups and connect with mentors, investors, and fellow business owners.

items.label: SBDCs
items.html: Local Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) — Visit americassbdc.org to find Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) that provide free business coaching, funding advice, and resources for entrepreneurs.

79122515.text: Tip: How to Approach These Organizations

79122515.html: Call first: Most grants require direct contact before applying. Call and explain your business idea.
Be persistent: Some programs might not be available in your area. Keep asking until you find the right fit.
Avoid Google scams: Many for-profit companies charge fees for grant applications — stick to nonprofit and government-backed resources.
This step sets you on the path to securing the funds you need for your business. Start calling today!

80037997.html: If you're struggling with debt or keeping up with bills, you're not alone. The stress of financial problems can affect your health, peace of mind, and overall well-being. The good news? There's free expert help available to guide you through the process. This lesson will show you where to start and how to avoid common pitfalls.

80037997.text: Make an Appointment With a Free Financial Counselor

80037997.html: Many people turn to Google for debt relief, but this can lead to scams or costly services. Instead, start by connecting with a certified financial counselor — many of them offer free, government-funded support. These experts can help you assess your financial situation, prioritize your debts, and create a realistic plan to regain control.
Here's how to find a trusted financial counselor:

items.label: Search
items.html: Visit HUD.gov/counseling and enter your zip code to find a HUD-approved financial counselor who specializes in debt management and credit counseling.

items.label: Locate
items.html: Pinpoint the application or contact information on the website of the HUD-approved financial counselor you have chosen, and follow the steps indicated to start the process of acquiring a counselor.

items.label: Check Email
items.html: A certified counseling agency will contact you to schedule an appointment — either in person, over the phone, or via Zoom meeting.

items.label: Gather Information
items.html: Prepare your financial documents, including bills, credit reports, and any notices from creditors.

80037997.html: Create folders (digital or physical) to keep all your financial information organized and easily accessible.

80037997.text: Seek Advice from More than One Expert

80037997.html: Not all counselors have the same knowledge or access to resources. If one doesn't provide the answers you need, don't hesitate to contact another. There are multiple government-backed programs and nonprofit organizations available to help.

Many online services charge fees for "debt relief" but fail to deliver. Some even engage in fraudulent practices. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) has banned over 450 debt relief companies from operating due to scams. Protect yourself by avoiding high-cost services and sticking to government-approved resources.

80037997.text: Use Trusted Websites for Financial Help

80037997.html: Taking this first step — getting expert, free guidance — will set you on the right path to reducing your debt and managing your bills effectively.

80037998.text: How to Negotiate Your Debt & Pay Less

80037998.html: Most people don't realize that debt is negotiable — creditors are often willing to settle for less because they just want to recover as much as possible. That means you have the power to reduce what you owe if you know how to approach it the right way.

Before you start negotiating, understand your rights and available strategies. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) offers a step-by-step guide on how to settle debt directly with creditors.

items.html: ConsumerFinance.gov – Visit ConsumerFinance.gov and search for "negotiate a settlement with your debt collector." This guide walks you through every step, from preparing for the call to finalizing an agreement.

NerdWallet's Debt Negotiation Guide – While they promote financial products, they have a useful guide on what to say when negotiating and how to settle your debt properly. Visit NerdWallet.com and search for "how to negotiate your debt."

80037998.text: Call Your Creditors & Make an Offer

80037998.html: Once you're prepared, it's time to negotiate:

items.html: Gather Your Financial Information – Know exactly how much you owe and to whom.
Make the Call – Contact your creditor and offer a lower amount (many will accept partial payments).
Explain Your Situation – If you're experiencing hardship, let them know. Some companies have hardship programs that reduce your debt or payment amount.
Get Everything in Writing – Once you agree on a settlement, ask for written confirmation before making any payments.

80037998.html: Many companies claim they can erase your debt but often charge hidden fees or fail to deliver results. Avoid third-party debt settlement services — you can negotiate directly with creditors for free.

Stick to .gov, .org, and .edu websites for reliable help. If a service asks for money upfront, walk away. (Be aware that some HUD Approved Counselors charge a small upfront fee. There will be options that do not charge a fee, the choice is yours.)
Every step you take brings you closer to financial freedom. By learning how to negotiate effectively, you can reduce your debt and regain control of your finances.
Start by reading the official negotiation guide at ConsumerFinance.gov
You got this! The sooner you start, the more you save.

80037999.text: How to Stop Bill Collectors from Harassing You – And Get Paid $1,000

80037999.html: Getting calls from debt collectors can be stressful, but you have rights—and knowing them can stop the harassment and even get you compensated. Some debt collectors break the law by using threats, intimidation, and deceptive tactics, but you don’t have to put up with it.
Here’s how to protect yourself and potentially get paid $1,000 if they violate your rights.
The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) protects you from abusive debt collection practices. Debt collectors CANNOT legally do the following:

items.html: Threaten you – They can’t say you’ll be arrested, deported, or sued unless it’s a legitimate legal case.
Harass you – No abusive language, constant calls, or intimidation.
Lie to you – They can’t pretend to be lawyers or government agents, or claim you owe money you don’t.
Call you at any time – They can’t call before 8 AM or after 9 PM without permission.
Tell others about your debt – They can’t contact your employer, family, or friends about your financial situation.

80037999.html: If a debt collector violates any of these rules, you can report them and potentially sue for damages.

items.html: ReportFraud.FTC.gov – The Federal Trade Commission investigates debt collector abuses.
ConsumerFinance.gov – The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau provides legal protections against unfair debt collection.

80037999.html: If you’re being harassed, you can legally make them stop. Send the debt collector a "Cease and Desist" letter, telling them to stop contacting you.
TIP: Keep a record of all calls and messages—this can be used as evidence if they break the law.
Find a sample letter here CaliforniaStateUniversityLongBeach.edu Debt Collection Letter Templates

80037999.text: How to Get Paid $1,000 If They Break the Law

80037999.html: If a debt collector violates your rights, you can sue them and may be awarded:

items.html: $1,000 in statutory damages (even if you didn’t suffer financial loss).
Additional compensation for mental or physical harm.
Attorney fees covered – meaning you won’t have to pay for legal help.

80037999.text: Get Free Legal Help to Fight Back

80037999.html: Don’t pay for a lawyer—there are free legal resources to help you fight unfair debt collection practices.

items.html: FindHelp.org – Search for pro bono lawyers in your area.
ConsumerFinance.gov – Learn how to take legal action and file a complaint.
Report illegal debt collection practices.
Send a Cease and Desist letter to stop the harassment.
Get legal help and sue if your rights have been violated.

80037999.html: Debt collectors rely on intimidation, but you have the law on your side. Take control, fight back, and don’t let them push you around.

80038000.html: Now that you understand your financial situation and know what’s possible, it’s time to take action and start securing the help you need.

This step focuses on contacting trusted organizations that provide grants, financial aid, and bill assistance programs. These programs can help with rent, mortgage payments, utilities, medical bills, taxes, and even debt forgiveness.

These programs are part of the giving economy — a network of government offices and nonprofits offering financial assistance at no cost. Unlike for-profit services on Google that charge fees, these organizations are designed to help, not profit from your situation.

items.label: FindHelp
items.html: FindHelp.org — Visit FindHelp.org and enter your zip code to access thousands of local programs that provide grants and free financial support for rent, utilities, mortgage, food, and more.

items.label: Student Loans
items.html: Student loan assistance (StudentAid.gov) — Visit StudentAid.gov to explore loan forgiveness, repayment plans, and relief programs for student debt. Call their helpline to understand your options.

items.label: IRS
items.html: IRS Offer in Compromise program — If you owe back taxes, the IRS can forgive up to 90% of your tax debt. Contact your local IRS office and ask about the Offer in Compromise program to see if you qualify.

items.label: State Taxes
items.html: State tax relief programs — Most states offer tax debt forgiveness programs. Contact your state comptroller or tax office to inquire about tax relief or hardship programs in your area. See the directory of State Tax Agencies.

items.label: Medical Bills
items.html: Medical bill assistance (Patient Advocate Foundation) — Visit the Patient Advocate Foundation for help with medical bill assistance, co-pay grants, and financial aid for healthcare costs.

items.label: PAN Foundation
items.html: PAN Foundation — Visit panfoundation.org to access financial assistance programs that help individuals cover out-of-pocket medical expenses, including prescription costs, insurance premiums, and treatment-related expenses.

items.label: NeedyMeds
items.html: NeedyMeds.org — Find free and low-cost prescription medication, medical services, and bill assistance at Needymeds.org or call 1-800-503-6897.

items.label: Hospital Bills
items.html: Hospital bill forgiveness (DollarFor.org) — Many hospitals are legally required to forgive medical bills based on income levels. Visit DollarFor.org to see if you qualify for hospital bill relief and how to apply.

items.label: Government Debt
items.html: Government & Social Security department assistance — If you owe unemployment insurance overpayments, Social Security repayments, or government loans, first contact the agency you owe — they often have hardship waivers or payment reductions. If they refuse to help, call your elected officials to advocate on your behalf.

items.label: Child Support
items.html: Back child support forgiveness — The Office of Child Support Services has state-by-state forgiveness programs that can reduce or eliminate child support debt. Check with your state child support office to see if you qualify.

items.label: Common Cause
items.html: Common Cause — If you’re struggling with government debts, fines, or legal financial obligations, your elected officials can intervene. Visit CommonCause.org to find who represents you and ask for their help in resolving financial hardships.

80038000.html: Call first — Most of these programs require direct communication. Call their offices, explain your situation, and ask for available assistance.
Be persistent — Not every program will be available in your area, so you may need to make multiple calls to find the right assistance.
Avoid Google searches — Many for-profit services pretend to be “helpful” but charge high fees. Stick to government-backed and nonprofit organizations for real support.

items.label: IRS Offer in Compromise (or contact your local IRS office)
State Tax Relief Programs — find your state tax department
Back Child Support Forgiveness — your state child support office

80038000.html: For government and Social Security debt, there is no website to start with: call the agency you owe first, then your elected official if they will not help.
These steps put you on the path to securing the financial help you need. Start calling today and take control of your debt!

80242726.html: Starting a nonprofit can be overwhelming—especially when looking for funding, legal guidance, and expert support. But here’s the secret: don’t start by searching on Google. Most results will be businesses trying to sell you something, not the free help you actually need.
Instead, go where nonprofits and government agencies provide expert assistance—for free.

80242802.html: Getting the healthcare you need shouldn’t be overwhelming or expensive. The good news? There are thousands of free and low-cost clinics that provide medical, dental, mental health, and substance use care—you just need to know where to look.
This lesson will guide you to the best resources for accessing affordable health care options near you.

80242802.text: Find Free and Low-Cost Clinics Near You

80242802.html: Many nonprofit organizations and government programs offer free or low-cost healthcare services. Here’s how to get started:

items.label: Search
items.html: Visit NeedyMeds.org and explore their Healthcare Savings section to find medical clinics, dental clinics, mental health clinics, and substance use disorder clinics.

items.label: Locate
items.html: Use the clinic directory to find options near you, and check their website for eligibility, services, and appointment availability.

items.label: Check email
items.html: After reaching out, you’ll receive an email with appointment details for in-person, phone, or online consultations.

items.label: Gather information
items.html: Organize your medical history, medications, and any questions about your health concerns before your appointment.

80242802.html: Keep all medical records and documents in one folder for easy access.

80242802.text: Apply for Low-Cost or Free Health Insurance

80242802.html: Even if you don’t think you qualify, 4 out of 5 applicants find coverage for less than $10 per month.

items.html: Visit HealthCare.gov to explore affordable insurance plans.
Get Free Help | Find Navigators or Certified Application Counselors who assist with applications at no cost: Find Free Application Help.

80242802.html: Avoid Agents & Brokers | These professionals work for insurance companies and may only offer plans that benefit them.
Mental health care is just as important as physical health. The government offers a judgment-free hotline to connect you with free or low-cost counselors:

items.html: Call 988 | Speak with a counselor online or schedule an in-person appointment near you.
Visit 988Lifeline.org for more information.

80242802.text: Learn About Clinical Trials for Free Care

80242802.html: If traditional healthcare isn’t working for you, clinical trials provide free access to cutting-edge treatments.

items.html: Explore ClinicalTrials.gov to find government-funded studies on new treatments and procedures. These can offer free treatment & care, access to top specialists, and compensation for travel & participation.
$50 billion is spent annually on clinical trials, providing free treatment by top doctors and researchers.

80242802.html: If you’re on Medicare, new benefits and changes happen frequently. Free experts are available to help explain what you’re entitled to.

items.html: Call 877-839-2675 to speak with a Medicare expert.
Visit SHIPHelp.org and find local Medicare advisors in your state.

80242802.text: Find Local Health Services in Your Area

80242802.html: For more free healthcare services in your area:

items.html: Go to FindHelp.org: Enter your ZIP code and click the Health tab to see available options.

80242802.html: There are over 215 sources of free healthcare in some areas—find out what’s available near you!

80242802.text: Key Resources for Finding Low-Cost Health Care

items.label: Apply for Affordable Health Insurance – HealthCare.gov
Find Free Application Help – Certified Navigators
Find a Clinical Trial for Free Treatment – ClinicalTrials.gov
Find More Local Health Services – FindHelp.org

80242802.html: These free and low-cost resources can help you stay healthy without breaking the bank. Start searching today!

83136879.html: Before you dive into applying for grants, building a brand, or launching your product, there are a few foundational steps you must take to officially set up your business.

This checklist will guide you through the essential legal and administrative actions needed to start strong. It includes everything from choosing your business structure to opening a bank account and securing licenses.

Important: In the United States, all business registrations and incorporations are handled on the state level. This means that fees, processes, and specific requirements vary depending on your state. We highly recommend checking with your state's Department of Commerce or Secretary of State to confirm details specific to your location.

Each item builds on the one before. Read through each step carefully and keep track of your progress. Items marked with * need to be renewed annually. Items marked with *? may have unique renewal timelines — check locally.

items.label: Name
items.html: Select your business name and legal structure. Decide on your business name and legal form: Sole Proprietorship, Partnership, LLC, or Corporation. This choice affects taxes, liability, and how you can raise funds.

items.label: Research
items.html: Research your business name with the Secretary of State. Research your business name on your state's Secretary of State website to make sure no other business has that name.

items.label: Register
items.html: Register the legal entity with your state. * File your business with the state government and obtain your Certificate of Incorporation or Articles of Organization.

items.label: State tax
items.html: Get your state tax license and set up tax accounts. Create a State Tax ID/account through your state's tax division. This is different from your federal EIN and is essential for state-level tax compliance.

items.label: Federal EIN
items.html: Obtain your federal EIN from the IRS. Apply online for your Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS. This is necessary to open bank accounts, hire employees, and file taxes.

items.label: Bank account
items.html: Open a business bank or credit union account. Set up a business checking account at a trusted FDIC-insured bank or credit union using your EIN and state paperwork.

items.label: Local license
items.html: Apply for a local business license. * Depending on your location, you'll need to register your business with your city or county office based on your physical address.

items.label: Permits
items.html: Get professional licenses or permits (if required). *? If your business operates in a regulated industry (like health, finance, childcare, or food services), you may need specific licenses or inspections. Renewal timelines vary, so always verify the terms for your specific license or permit.

This lesson will guide you through some of the most important federal and city-level resources you can use as a small business owner. Whether you’re looking for government contracts, certifications, or simply trying to locate your local support agency, this is a great place to start.
These government-run offices are designed to support small business participation in federal programs, including funding, contracts, and training.

items.html: Federal Small Business Offices — Explore how to work with the U.S. Department of Defense and connect with federal small business representatives in various agencies.

83136916.html: These general portals can guide you to many different government services and small business tools:

items.html: USA.gov Small Business Portal — A great all-in-one resource for exploring small business programs, licenses, and government-run support.
MySBA Certifications — Looking to become a certified small business for federal contracts or programs? This is the official SBA platform to get started with certifications.

83136916.text: Local Government Tools: Find Help in Your Area

83136916.html: Local programs are often easier to access and more tailored to your needs. These tools will help you find your county, city, and regional offices, where additional grants, licenses, or support may be offered.

83137118.html: Not every great idea fits the mold—and not every business needs a bank loan or venture capital to grow. Non-traditional funding opens doors through alternative pathways like crowdfunding, pitch competitions, revenue-based financing, community development funds, peer-to-peer lending, and even business grants from brands or nonprofits.

These options often provide more flexibility, less pressure, and a stronger alignment with mission-driven or underserved entrepreneurs—making them ideal for founders who want creative capital without giving up control.

83137128.html: Crowdfunding is a modern way to raise money for your business by rallying support from individuals who believe in your idea — whether they are future customers, friends, family, or total strangers. It works especially well when you have a compelling story, a passionate mission, or a product people are excited about.
There are different types of crowdfunding:

items.html: Donation-based (people support you without expecting anything in return)
Reward-based (supporters get early access, perks, or products)
Equity-based (backers become investors in your company)
Debt-based (you repay the funds like a loan)

83646154.html: Did you know that the U.S. government is the largest buyer of goods and services in the world? Every year, billions of dollars in contracts are awarded to small businesses—just like yours. Whether you offer products, services, consulting, or manufacturing, government contracting can open a stable and lucrative revenue stream.

But breaking into federal, state, or local contracting requires understanding the process, registering correctly, and knowing where to look. This guide will walk you through the essential steps and tools to get started.

83646154.text: 1. Register Your Business on SAM.gov (Your First Step)

83646154.html: Before you can bid on federal contracts or subcontracts, you must register your business on SAM.gov. This is the official database where all contractors are listed.

items.html: Entity Checklist — Before registering, download the Entity Checklist (PDF) on SAM.gov to prepare all required documents.
Search Contracts — Even before you’re fully registered, browse available contracts to get familiar with opportunities.

83646154.html: Start here: SAM.gov Registration & Search

83646154.text: 2. Know Your Codes: NAICS, PSC & UNSPSC

83646154.html: Government agencies use specific codes to classify businesses and their services/products. You’ll need these during registration and bidding.

items.html: NAICS Codes — The North American Industry Classification System assigns a 6-digit number to describe your industry.
The following resources have both free and for-cost services. Please stick to the free resources: https://www.naics.com/ and https://naicscode.com/
PSC Codes — Product Service Codes (PSC) describe exactly what goods or services you’re offering.
UNSPSC Codes — Some agencies may also require UNSPSC Codes for additional classification.

83646154.html: Make sure you’ve identified the correct codes before completing your SAM registration.
You don’t have to navigate government contracting alone. APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) offer free counseling to help small businesses understand and succeed in federal contracting.

items.html: Learn how to bid
Understand compliance rules
Get help with certifications

83646154.html: Find a counselor near you: APEX Accelerators
The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) offers powerful tools to help you access set-aside contracts and navigate the system.

items.html: Size Standards Tool — Check if your business qualifies as a “small business” for federal contracting purposes. Use the Tool
SBA Contracting Assistance Programs — Explore programs like 8(a), HUBZone, and WOSB certifications to access exclusive contract opportunities. Learn More

83646154.html: If you’re contracting with the Department of Defense or its agencies, you’ll likely need to register on the Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment (PIEE) to receive payments.
For other agencies, payment systems will vary—always confirm with the awarding agency which platform to use.

83646154.text: 6. Learn the Rules: Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR)

83646154.html: The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) outlines how federal contracts are issued and managed. It’s complex, so reviewing it with an APEX Accelerator counselor is highly recommended.
Get ahead by knowing what agencies are buying and who they’re buying from:

items.html: Agency Recurring Procurement Forecasts — See what agencies plan to purchase in upcoming cycles.
USA Spending — Track past contracts: who won them and for how much.
D-U-N-S Number — While no longer required for SAM.gov, many other agencies still ask for a D-U-N-S number. It’s like a Social Security number for your business, so it’s good to have on hand.
Gather your documents using the SAM.gov Entity Checklist.
Identify your NAICS, PSC, and (if needed) UNSPSC codes.
Register on SAM.gov and book a free session with your local APEX Accelerator counselor.
Explore SBA’s contracting assistance programs to see if you qualify for set-asides.

83646154.html: Government contracting can feel overwhelming at first, but with the right steps and support, it becomes a powerful way to grow your business.
Once you’re registered and familiar with the process, start bidding on smaller contracts to build experience, and watch new doors open.
